newsitem.title: BOSNIA: World Bank urges cut in Bosnian payroll tax.
newsitem.headline: World Bank urges cut in Bosnian payroll tax.

text.p: A World Bank official said on Tuesday that Bosnia urgently needed to reform its steep payroll tax to encourage job growth in a post-war economy plagued by high unemployment.

Bosnia's 100 percent employment tax was counter-productive at a time when international donors were pouring reconstruction funds into Bosnia to create jobs, Rory O'Sulllivan, chief of the World Bank office in Sarajevo.
For every 100 German marks a worker was paid the employer had to pay another 100 marks in tax.
"If you had to design a policy which would prevent employment that's the very policy you would put into place, a 100 percent employment tax," O'Sullivan told a news conference.
He said the World Bank would propose a reform of the payroll tax and the entire tax system in Bosnia to create conditions for economic growth and job creation.
The payroll tax should probably be cut to about 25 percent, which O'Sullivan called a more realistic level.
The current tax was so high that it "encourages fraud," O'Sullivan said.
Reconstruction aid for Bosnia had been aimed primarily at creating jobs in a country with large numbers of demobilised soldiers.
Authorities said they had no clear estimate of the number of unemployed but 43 months of war had left most of the population jobless.
The World Bank estimates that more than 200,000 jobs were created last year through reconstruction assistance, O'Sullivan said.
Many of those jobs were temporary and reconstruction efforts were now focused on pushing for economic reforms that would pave the way for long-term employment, he said.
The World Bank and other foreign experts were also recommending harmonising various import and excise duties.
"The whole question of tax has to be sorted out," O'Sullivan told Reuters after the press conference.
"We are aiming at a flat eight to 10 percent import duty without exemptions," he said. "You actually get more revenue that way, once you get rid of all the exceptions everybody pays."
Currently there are a range of restrictions on different imports, particularly in Bosnia's Serb republic, and rates range from eight to 20 percent depending on the item.

Revenues for customs and excise duties for Bosnia's Moslem- Croat federation will probably come to some 280 million German marks ($190 million) for 1996, according preliminary estimates, the World Bank said.
The German mark is commonly used in Bosnia. ($1=1.5867 Mark)
